_note: Situations grounded in the ODL PM, Learning Design and Media SOPs. Each has exactly one full-credit answer; other answers earn partial credit and explain why in 'why'. 'who' is the person shown; 'mood' their face when the situation appears; 'reaction' their face after the choice.

events.title: Tomorrow's Meeting Has No Agenda
events.text: Priya stops by: "Tomorrow's content mapping meeting with Dr. Ward is our first real working session. Is there an agenda? I need her to bring her old syllabus and her top three outcomes."

choices.label: Draft the agenda with Priya today, list what Dr. Ward should bring, and send it with the materials so she can prepare.
choices.outcome: Dr. Ward arrives with her syllabus and outcomes. The meeting ends early with decisions made.
choices.why: The SOP asks the PM to draft every agenda with the lead designer or producer and share materials ahead, especially for busy faculty.

choices.label: Write a quick agenda yourself and send it tomorrow morning.
choices.outcome: The agenda goes out, but Dr. Ward hasn't seen it before the meeting and arrives without her syllabus.
choices.why: Having an agenda helps, but it missed Priya's goals for the meeting and gave the faculty no time to prepare.

choices.label: Skip the agenda; it's a casual first meeting.
choices.outcome: The hour drifts. You leave with a second meeting to schedule.
choices.why: Meetings without an agenda wander, and faculty time is the scarcest resource on the project.

choices.label: Postpone the meeting a week so there's time to prepare.
choices.outcome: You get prepared, but lose a week of design time and Dr. Ward has to rearrange her calendar.
choices.why: A day is enough time to draft an agenda; moving the meeting costs schedule and goodwill.

debrief.concept: Meetings are the PM's main tool. Prepare them so faculty time isn't wasted.
debrief.independent: Agree the meeting goals with the lead designer, draft the agenda from the template, and send it with any materials a day or more ahead.
debrief.escalateWhen: Not an escalation issue. This is core PM work.
debrief.sop: PM SOP: Managing Meetings, Meeting agendas

events.title: Can We Just Move the Date?
events.text: Priya needs one more week on the course map. "Can you just slide it in Asana? It's only a week." The timeline was reviewed by the ODL directors last month.

choices.label: Map the knock-on effects with Priya and Marcus, propose how to absorb them, then take the change to the directors for approval before updating Asana.
choices.outcome: The directors approve a one-week shift with scripting starting in parallel. Everyone sees the same dates.
choices.why: Once a timeline is established, changes need director review. Bringing the knock-on effects and a plan is exactly how to ask.

choices.label: Slide the date in Asana. It's only a week.
choices.outcome: Asana updates. Marcus finds out two weeks later that scripting now collides with another shoot.
choices.why: Quiet changes skip the approval the SOP requires and hide knock-on effects from the rest of the team.

choices.label: Hold the date. Ask Priya to finish on time.
choices.outcome: Priya delivers on time, but the assessment plan is thin.
choices.why: Holding a date by pressure alone moves the problem into quality.

choices.label: Keep the date by finishing the assessment plan later, during development.
choices.outcome: The course map lands on time; the assessment work shifts into development.
choices.why: A sensible trade-off, but it changes the plan without the team or directors agreeing to it.

choices.label: Tell Jordan that Priya wants more time and ask what to do.
choices.outcome: Jordan asks what the change affects. You don't know yet.
choices.why: Escalating is right here, but bring the impact and a recommendation, not just the request.

debrief.concept: Change control: know who approves timeline changes, and surface knock-on effects before asking.
debrief.independent: Meet with the affected people, review the timeline, list knock-on effects and how to absorb them. Then get a clear approval and update Asana.
debrief.escalateWhen: Here escalation is required: established timelines change only with director approval. Come with the analysis.
debrief.sop: PM SOP: Design phase; When Things Go Wrong, With Timelines

events.title: The Scripting Workshop Gets Heated
events.text: Forty minutes into the scripting workshop, Dr. Ward and Marcus are arguing about tone. She wants formal lectures; he's pitching the conversational style from the lookbook. Half the agenda is untouched.

choices.label: Restate the meeting goals, summarize both views, and park the tone question for a short follow-up where Marcus shows two sample clips.
choices.outcome: The room calms down. You finish the agenda, and the sample clips settle tone the next week.
choices.why: The SOP's first move: remind everyone of the objectives, summarize, and refocus. Parking the debate keeps the meeting productive.

choices.label: Professionally end the meeting and reschedule.
choices.outcome: Things cool off, but you lose the rest of the agenda and a week of scripting.
choices.why: Ending a meeting is a valid SOP option when it's unproductive, but try refocusing first.

choices.label: Side with Dr. Ward. It's her course.
choices.outcome: Dr. Ward is satisfied. Marcus goes quiet for the rest of the meeting.
choices.why: The PM facilitates; picking a side undermines the producer's expertise and skips the evidence.

choices.label: Let them work it out; creative tension is healthy.
choices.outcome: The meeting runs over and ends without decisions.
choices.why: Keeping meetings on task is the PM's job.

choices.label: After the meeting, ask Jordan to step in on the tone decision.
choices.outcome: Jordan suggests the sample-clip approach you could have proposed in the room.
choices.why: This is a facilitation problem you can handle. Escalate only if the disagreement persists.

debrief.concept: Facilitation: restate goals, summarize, refocus, and know when to end a meeting.
debrief.independent: Remind people what the meeting is for, summarize where things stand, and move the disagreement to a follow-up with evidence (sample clips, lookbook). End the meeting professionally if it keeps going sideways, and do an internal touchbase before the next one.
debrief.escalateWhen: Bring in ODL leadership when a disagreement keeps blocking decisions across meetings.
debrief.sop: PM SOP: When Things Go Wrong, In Meetings

events.title: Silent Faculty
events.text: Dr. Ward hasn't answered Priya's or Marcus's last emails. Scripts are due in two weeks. Priya: "I've sent three messages. Marcus sent two of his own."

choices.label: Route all requests through you, and propose a standing 15-minute Friday check-in plus comments in the script Google Docs.
choices.outcome: Dr. Ward accepts the Friday slot. Fewer emails, faster answers.
choices.why: For hard-to-reach faculty the SOP says streamline communication through as few people as possible, limit emails, and use short check-ins and async comments.

choices.label: Send one long email listing everything the team needs from her.
choices.outcome: She replies to the first item and misses the rest.
choices.why: One channel is better, but a long list buries the asks.

choices.label: Ask Priya and Marcus to each follow up again.
choices.outcome: Dr. Ward now has seven unread emails from ODL.
choices.why: More senders means more noise. This is the opposite of what the SOP recommends.

choices.label: Brief Jordan on the risk to the script deadline, what's been tried, and your proposed check-in plan.
choices.outcome: Jordan agrees with your plan and suggests you try it first.
choices.why: A solid escalation, but this is a communication fix within your control.

choices.label: Forward the thread to Jordan: "Faculty isn't responding."
choices.outcome: Jordan asks what you've tried and what you recommend.
choices.why: Escalating without options hands the thinking upward.

choices.label: Wait. She's probably just busy with midterms.
choices.outcome: Another week passes in silence.
choices.why: Waiting lets the risk grow.

debrief.concept: Stakeholder communication: fit the channel to the person.
debrief.independent: Find out how the faculty member prefers to communicate. Funnel requests through one person, keep emails few and short, and use brief standing check-ins and doc comments.
debrief.escalateWhen: Bring in ODL leadership when silence persists after you've changed the approach and the delivery date is at risk.
debrief.sop: PM SOP: Challenging Faculty; Faculty Availability

events.title: Dr. Ward Is Drowning
events.text: Dr. Ward emails late at night: "Scripts, quiz questions and reading lists are all due the same week as my midterms. I can't do all of this."

choices.label: Re-pace with Priya and Marcus: stagger the deadlines, and have Priya draft quiz questions from the course map for her to edit.
choices.outcome: "This I can do." Her drafts start arriving again.
choices.why: The SOP asks the PM to watch faculty pacing, and to work offline on drafts the faculty can react to.

choices.label: Push all her deadlines back two weeks.
choices.outcome: She's relieved, but production and the build now start late.
choices.why: Moving everything ignores the knock-on effects on media and design, and skips approval.

choices.label: Remind her the charter set these dates.
choices.outcome: She goes quiet.
choices.why: The charter matters, but this is a pacing problem the team can solve together.

choices.label: Ask Jordan for approval to re-sequence her deliverables, with a proposed staggered schedule.
choices.outcome: Jordan approves. The new schedule helps, a few days later than it could have.
choices.why: Fine if the re-pace changes milestone dates; otherwise you can rearrange within the window yourself.

debrief.concept: Pace the faculty: steady progress beats a pile-up.
debrief.independent: Stagger asks, let designers and producers draft so faculty only react, and keep the delivery date fixed while moving work within it.
debrief.escalateWhen: Escalate if re-pacing moves established milestones; those need director approval.
debrief.sop: PM SOP: Development phase note on pacing; Faculty Availability

events.title: The 5-Minute Video Is 14 Minutes
events.text: Marcus is reviewing scripts: "Module 3 reads at about 14 minutes. The charter says 5-minute videos. She's attached to every word."

choices.label: Remind Dr. Ward the charter commits to 5-minute videos and make trimming a priority, with Marcus marking which parts could move to a reading.
choices.outcome: She trims to 6 minutes and moves the rest to a reading. Marcus can live with 6.
choices.why: This is the SOP's own example: point to the charter, prioritize the trim, and offer an in-scope alternative.

choices.label: Split it into two videos.
choices.outcome: Everyone's happy until post-production runs long.
choices.why: It adds a deliverable that isn't in the charter.

choices.label: Film it as written and cut it down in editing.
choices.outcome: The shoot runs long and the edit becomes a puzzle.
choices.why: Problems left in the script get more expensive in production and post.

choices.label: Ask Marcus to rewrite it shorter himself.
choices.outcome: Dr. Ward rejects the rewrite as "not my voice."
choices.why: Producers review scripts, but the content belongs to the faculty member.

choices.label: Ask Jordan to talk to Dr. Ward about the length.
choices.outcome: Jordan points back to the charter, just as you could have.
choices.why: Scope reminders are the PM's job first. Escalate if creep keeps coming back.

debrief.concept: Scope: the charter is your tool for holding the line kindly.
debrief.independent: Refer to the charter, make the fix an action item, and offer an in-scope alternative (move detail to a reading or the LMS).
debrief.escalateWhen: If scope creep persists, work with the practice area directors to find the cause; in the worst case escalate to the ODL director.
debrief.sop: PM SOP: Change of Scope

events.title: Can We Add a Simulation?
events.text: Dr. Ward saw a colleague's custom interactive brain simulation. "Can we build one for Module 5? It would be perfect." It isn't in the charter.

choices.label: Ask what she wants students to learn from it, then have Priya propose a way to meet that goal directly in Canvas.
choices.outcome: Priya designs a labelled-diagram activity in Canvas. Dr. Ward likes it, and nothing new goes into scope.
choices.why: The SOP suggests discussing ways to reach the goal directly on the LMS when an interactive isn't in scope.

choices.label: Say yes. It'll make the course stand out.
choices.outcome: Dr. Ward is thrilled. Marcus is now animating on top of eight videos.
choices.why: Out-of-scope work with no trade-off lands on the team and the schedule.

choices.label: Tell her it's out of scope.
choices.outcome: Correct, but she feels shut down.
choices.why: Scope holds, but without an alternative it costs trust.

choices.label: Log it as a possible future project after launch.
choices.outcome: She agrees to revisit after launch.
choices.why: Good scope control; even better is meeting the learning goal now within scope.

choices.label: Ask Jordan whether ODL can take on the extra work.
choices.outcome: Jordan asks whether you explored an in-scope option first.
choices.why: Explore in-scope options before asking for more resources.

debrief.concept: Scope: go back to the learning goal behind the request.
debrief.independent: Ask what the request is for. Propose an in-scope way to reach the same goal, often directly in the LMS.
debrief.escalateWhen: Escalate when the faculty member insists on out-of-scope work after you've offered alternatives.
debrief.sop: PM SOP: Change of Scope

events.title: Somebody Else Booked the Studio
events.text: Marcus: "The studio and two of our crew are booked for another project on our shoot days. Our dates were never blocked on the media calendar."

choices.label: Book the next open dates and block every remaining production day on the media calendar now. Have Priya build the master site with video placeholders meanwhile.
choices.outcome: You lose a week of shooting, but the build keeps moving and it won't happen again.
choices.why: Blocking production days is a PM duty in the SOP; re-sequencing keeps the rest of the team productive.

choices.label: Book the next open dates.
choices.outcome: New dates are set. The other remaining days are still unblocked.
choices.why: Fixes today's problem but not the cause.

choices.label: Ask Marcus to shoot on a Saturday.
choices.outcome: The shoot happens, with a tired crew.
choices.why: Overtime as a first resort costs morale and quality.

choices.label: Ask Jordan and the directors whether the other project can swap a day, with the impact on our launch.
choices.outcome: The other project swaps one day. You still need to block the rest.
choices.why: Reasonable for a shared-resource conflict, but the root cause, blocking calendars, is yours to fix.

choices.label: Wait for the studio to free up.
choices.outcome: Three weeks pass before the cameras roll.
choices.why: Production sits on the critical path; waiting moves the launch.

debrief.concept: Protect the critical path: production dates are scarce.
debrief.independent: As soon as production dates are known, block them on the media team's calendar. When a path stalls, re-sequence other work (placeholders in the master site).
debrief.escalateWhen: Escalate for shared-resource conflicts you can't resolve with the other project's PM.
debrief.sop: PM SOP: Design phase (block media calendars); LD SOP: placeholders

events.title: Two Videos Will Be a Week Late
events.text: Marcus: "Modules 7 and 8 will be a week late. The audio from the shoot needs more cleanup than I planned."

choices.label: Meet with Marcus and Priya, check that Priya still has time to place the videos before launch, have her finish the rest of the site first, then get a clear change approval and update Asana.
choices.outcome: Priya reorders her build. The late videos slot in with days to spare.
choices.why: This is the SOP's worked example: surface knock-on effects, let design prioritize the rest of the LMS, document the change.

choices.label: Update the dates in Asana.
choices.outcome: Priya notices the new dates a week later.
choices.why: Silent date changes skip the conversation about knock-on effects.

choices.label: Ask Marcus to hit the original date anyway.
choices.outcome: The videos arrive on time with audio issues QA will find.
choices.why: Pressure shifts the problem into quality.

choices.label: Ask the directors whether another producer can take some editing.
choices.outcome: A second editor helps for two weeks.
choices.why: A valid SOP option when internal changes can't be accommodated; here a re-sequence would have been enough.

debrief.concept: Knock-on effects: every slip lands on someone downstream.
debrief.independent: Meet with the affected team, review the timeline, surface knock-on effects, and make them manageable (re-order the build). Get clear approval, then update Asana.
debrief.escalateWhen: When the change can't be absorbed internally, work with the directors on shifting work between team members or revising scope.
debrief.sop: PM SOP: When Things Go Wrong, With Timelines

events.title: Forty Notes on Rough Cut 2
events.text: Dr. Ward sent 40 notes on Rough Cut 2. About half are fixes; the other half rewrite content she approved in the script.

choices.label: Meet with Dr. Ward and Marcus to sort fixes from new content. Schedule one more rough cut for fixes; move new content to a reading or after launch.
choices.outcome: A third rough cut handles the fixes. The new material becomes a short reading.
choices.why: The media SOP allows extra rough cuts when notes keep coming; the charter and approved scripts define what counts as a fix.

choices.label: Apply all 40 notes.
choices.outcome: Marcus starts re-editing whole sections.
choices.why: Treating new content as fixes is scope creep at the most expensive stage.

choices.label: Email her that only fixes will be applied.
choices.outcome: Right call, rough delivery. She feels dismissed.
choices.why: The decision is right; a conversation with an alternative would have kept trust.

choices.label: Send the notes to Jordan to decide.
choices.outcome: Jordan asks you to sort them first.
choices.why: Sorting notes is PM and producer work.

debrief.concept: Review windows: separate fixes from changes.
debrief.independent: Sort feedback into fixes and new requests, use extra rough cuts for fixes, and redirect new content using the charter.
debrief.escalateWhen: Escalate if late-stage changes keep threatening the delivery date.
debrief.sop: Media SOP: 4M Post-Production; PM SOP: Change of Scope

events.title: "Nobody Told Me Scripts Were Due"
events.text: Dr. Ward: "I didn't know scripts were due this week." The deadline was in three meeting summary emails.

choices.label: Learn how she reads email. Move key asks and dates to the top of the Friday weekly summary, and share a one-page development timeline.
choices.outcome: She reads Friday summaries. Deadlines stop being surprises.
choices.why: The SOP: find out which emails a faculty member reads, put careful thought into the weekly summary, and use a development timeline to track progress.

choices.label: Forward the three emails that mentioned the deadline.
choices.outcome: Technically right. Relationship worse.
choices.why: Proving you sent it doesn't fix how she receives information.

choices.label: Send a reminder email before every deadline from now on.
choices.outcome: More emails, some of which she reads.
choices.why: Adding email volume works against busy faculty.

choices.label: Copy her department chair on future reminders.
choices.outcome: She feels policed.
choices.why: Going around a partner damages trust and isn't how ODL escalates.

debrief.concept: Communication: match the channel to how the person actually reads.
debrief.independent: Ask which messages they read; use meeting summaries and Friday weekly summaries deliberately, lead with asks and dates, and share a visible development timeline.
debrief.escalateWhen: Not an escalation issue unless deadlines keep slipping after you've adapted.
debrief.sop: PM SOP: Summary emails; Challenging Faculty

events.title: Priya Is Stretched Thin
events.text: Priya mentions she's lead designer on four other courses. Her milestone check-ins have gotten shorter, and the master site is behind.

choices.label: Hold a 1:1, agree what this course needs from her each week, and simplify the module template to cut non-essential build work.
choices.outcome: Priya is relieved. A simpler template saves hours.
choices.why: Early, direct conversations and small scope trims protect both quality and morale.

choices.label: Bring Jordan Priya's workload and ask whether a supporting designer can help for a month.
choices.outcome: A supporting designer takes two modules.
choices.why: Good: cross-project workload is a leadership decision. Talking to Priya first would have been better.

choices.label: Remind her of the deadline and ask her to push through.
choices.outcome: She works late. Mistakes pile up quietly.
choices.why: Overload shows up as errors before it shows up as missed dates.

choices.label: Offer to build some Canvas pages yourself.
choices.outcome: Kind, but Priya now has to check your pages against the design.
choices.why: Doing team members' work pulls the PM off coordination and often adds rework.

debrief.concept: Team health: overload causes errors first and delays second.
debrief.independent: Talk early, agree priorities, and trim polish that doesn't serve learning.
debrief.escalateWhen: Escalate when overload comes from other projects; shifting work across people is decided with the directors.
debrief.sop: PM SOP: With Timelines (shifting work between team members)

events.title: No Captions Ordered
events.text: Priya: "The first videos are in Panopto, but no captions were ordered. I can't embed them until they're accessible."

choices.label: Have Marcus order and QA captions now, and add the distribution checklist (upload, captions, thumbnails, embed codes) to every video's task in Asana.
choices.outcome: Captions arrive in days, and the checklist catches the remaining videos.
choices.why: Captions ordered and QA'd are part of the media SOP's distribution step; making the checklist visible prevents repeats.

choices.label: Use Panopto's automatic captions without review.
choices.outcome: Fast, but psychology terms come out garbled.
choices.why: Captions must be QA'd, not just generated.

choices.label: Launch without captions and add them later.
choices.outcome: QA will flag every video.
choices.why: Accessibility is a launch requirement.

choices.label: Ask Priya to post transcripts instead.
choices.outcome: Priya loses a day doing media work.
choices.why: Transcripts are part of distribution, which belongs to media.

debrief.concept: Quality is planned in: use the checklist, every time.
debrief.independent: Hold media to the distribution checklist for every asset, and track it where the team works.
debrief.escalateWhen: Escalate if captioning services or budget are unavailable.
debrief.sop: Media SOP: 7M Distribution

events.title: Where Are the Embed Codes?
events.text: Priya has been hunting through Slack and Panopto for an hour: the embed codes and in-video quiz timestamps were never shared.

choices.label: Ask Marcus to document every embed code and quiz timestamp in the shared learning asset list, and make that the handoff point from now on.
choices.outcome: One list, one place. Priya embeds the rest in an afternoon.
choices.why: The media SOP has producers document embed codes and share them with the designer; the LD SOP's asset list is the natural home.

choices.label: Let Priya keep looking; she'll find them.
choices.outcome: She finds most of them.
choices.why: Handoffs that depend on hunting cost the downstream person time.

choices.label: Ask Marcus to Slack Priya the codes.
choices.outcome: Solved for today; next batch, same problem.
choices.why: Fixes the instance, not the handoff.

debrief.concept: Handoffs: define where work passes from one team to another.
debrief.independent: Agree one shared place (the asset list) where media hands assets to design, and make it part of the checklist.
debrief.escalateWhen: Not an escalation issue.
debrief.sop: Media SOP: 7M Distribution; LD SOP: Milestone 3 asset list

events.title: The Guest Didn't Sign a Release
events.text: Dr. Ward brought a graduate student on camera for a demonstration. Marcus just realized there's no signed release form.

choices.label: Get the release signed before any cut is shared, name it to convention, file it in the project's Admin folder, and add releases to the production checklist.
choices.outcome: Signed the next day. Nothing delayed.
choices.why: Release forms are a pre-production step in the media SOP, and the PM SOP names where they're stored.

choices.label: Use the footage; she's a student here.
choices.outcome: The footage goes in without permission.
choices.why: Using someone's likeness without a release is a real risk to the university.

choices.label: Cut the demonstration.
choices.outcome: Safe, but the module loses its best moment.
choices.why: Getting the signature would have kept it.

choices.label: Ask Jordan how to handle it.
choices.outcome: Jordan says: get it signed.
choices.why: The process is documented; you can follow it.

debrief.concept: Risk: paperwork before publishing.
debrief.independent: Collect releases before anyone appears on camera when possible, and always before footage is shared. File them by the naming convention.
debrief.escalateWhen: Escalate if the person refuses to sign and the footage is essential.
debrief.sop: Media SOP: 2M Release Forms; PM SOP: Google Drive structure

events.title: Who Owns These Videos?
events.text: Dr. Ward asks whether she can reuse the lecture videos if she moves to another university. No IP agreement has been drafted.

choices.label: Draft the IP agreement from past examples and the university policy, and finalize it with the ODL director.
choices.outcome: She gets a clear answer in writing within two weeks.
choices.why: Drafting IP agreements during development is a PM responsibility in the SOP, finalized with the director.

choices.label: Tell her the university owns everything.
choices.outcome: That's not necessarily what the policy says, and now she's upset.
choices.why: Never answer legal-ish questions from memory.

choices.label: Tell her you'll ask the director.
choices.outcome: The director asks you to draft it.
choices.why: The director finalizes, but the PM drafts.

choices.label: Say you'll sort it out after launch.
choices.outcome: She hesitates to approve the final cuts.
choices.why: Unresolved rights questions stall approvals.

debrief.concept: Agreements protect everyone: get rights in writing during development.
debrief.independent: Draft from the template and past examples, check the university IP policy, and review with the ODL director.
debrief.escalateWhen: The director finalizes the agreement; you bring the draft.
debrief.sop: PM SOP: Development (IP agreements)

events.title: Copyright Snag
events.text: A textbook chapter and two figures Dr. Ward relies on can't be posted in the online course as files.

choices.label: Ask the library about library reserves or linking, have Priya add a placeholder, and bring Dr. Ward open alternatives for the figures.
choices.outcome: Library reserves cover the chapter; open figures replace the rest.
choices.why: Go to the specialists, and bring the faculty member choices. The LD SOP already plans placeholders for library reserves.

choices.label: Post them anyway; only enrolled students can see them.
choices.outcome: It goes in. QA will flag it.
choices.why: Restricted access doesn't make posting legal.

choices.label: Drop the chapter and figures.
choices.outcome: Clean, but Dr. Ward has to rework the module.
choices.why: Removing content without alternatives hurts the course.

choices.label: Ask Jordan what to do.
choices.outcome: Jordan points you to the library.
choices.why: Know your campus experts and go to them directly.

debrief.concept: Risk: know your campus experts and bring alternatives.
debrief.independent: Go to the people who own the question (library, copyright), and offer the faculty member options rather than a problem.
debrief.escalateWhen: Escalate if the faculty member refuses compliant alternatives.
debrief.sop: LD SOP: Development (placeholders for library reserves)

events.title: Set Up the Publisher Homework Tool
events.text: Dr. Ward wants Priya to configure the textbook publisher's homework tool in the master site this week.

choices.label: Add a placeholder in the master site, and document in the hand-off guide that the instructor of record activates and configures it on the live site.
choices.outcome: Layout complete; setup steps are written for her term.
choices.why: The LD SOP: external tools get placeholders and are configured by the instructor of record on the live site.

choices.label: Have Priya configure it now.
choices.outcome: It's set up in the master site, then breaks when migrated.
choices.why: Tool configuration belongs on the live site, by the instructor of record.

choices.label: Tell her that's her job.
choices.outcome: True, unhelpfully put.
choices.why: Explain the process and support her with hand-off documentation.

debrief.concept: Know the boundaries: what ODL builds and what the instructor owns.
debrief.independent: Use placeholders and clear hand-off documentation for tools the instructor configures.
debrief.escalateWhen: Not an escalation issue.
debrief.sop: LD SOP: Master Site Completion

events.title: Launch Is Close and No Hand-off Is Scheduled
events.text: Jordan asks: "When's the hand-off meeting with Dr. Ward? Is the hand-off document started?" Neither is.

choices.label: Schedule the hand-off meeting now, and start the hand-off document with Priya (deliverables, maintenance instructions, resources), with the design document and links to every deliverable.
choices.outcome: Dr. Ward blocks the time. The document is ready before the meeting.
choices.why: The PM SOP's delivery checklist: hand-off document with the lead designer, all deliverables compiled, PM runs the meeting.

choices.label: Email Dr. Ward the course link on launch day.
choices.outcome: She has a course but no idea how to maintain it.
choices.why: A link isn't a hand-off.

choices.label: Ask Priya to handle the hand-off.
choices.outcome: Priya does it on top of QA.
choices.why: The designer drafts with you, but the PM owns the hand-off meeting.

debrief.concept: Delivery: finish the project, not just the course.
debrief.independent: Plan the hand-off weeks ahead: document, deliverables, meeting, follow-ups. Then run the retrospective.
debrief.escalateWhen: Not an escalation issue.
debrief.sop: PM SOP: Delivery; Retrospective

events.title: QA Turns Up a Pile of Issues
events.text: Priya's first QA pass on the live course found broken links, two quizzes with wrong settings, and a module unpublished. Launch is days away.

choices.label: Triage with Priya: fix launch-blocking issues first (settings, publishing, links in Module 1), log the rest with owners, and re-run the QA checklist before launch.
choices.outcome: Blockers are fixed in a day; the rest are scheduled and tracked.
choices.why: The LD SOP's QA step covers content, technology and platform with a checklist; triage protects launch day.

choices.label: Ask Priya to fix everything before doing anything else.
choices.outcome: Everything gets fixed, slowly, with the critical items mixed in with cosmetic ones.
choices.why: Fixing all of it is fine, but without priorities the launch-blocking issues wait in line.

choices.label: Launch as is and patch during week one.
choices.outcome: Students find the broken quiz first.
choices.why: Known issues at launch hit students and the faculty member's first impression.

choices.label: Tell Jordan and ask whether launch should move.
choices.outcome: Jordan asks which issues actually block launch.
choices.why: Moving a term launch is rarely an option; triage first, then escalate if blockers remain.

debrief.concept: Launch readiness: separate blockers from polish.
debrief.independent: Run the QA checklist early, triage by impact on students, assign owners, and re-check before launch.
debrief.escalateWhen: Escalate if launch-blocking issues can't be fixed before the course opens.
debrief.sop: LD SOP: Step 4 Implementation, QA checks

events.title: A New Module, Two Weeks Out
events.text: Dr. Ward: "I just got back from a conference. I want to add a module on a new study everyone's talking about. Just one short video and a reading?"

choices.label: Acknowledge the idea, point to the charter's eight modules, and offer to add it as an announcement and reading now with a full module considered for next term.
choices.outcome: She posts it as a discussion prompt and adds the module to her wish list.
choices.why: Hold scope with the charter and offer an in-scope way to include the idea now.

choices.label: Say yes; it's just one video.
choices.outcome: Marcus books an extra shoot two weeks before launch.
choices.why: A small yes late in development costs the most.

choices.label: Agree to add a reading only.
choices.outcome: A reading gets added; she's mostly satisfied.
choices.why: A good compromise, but it still changes scope without referencing the charter or the team.

choices.label: Tell her you'll check with Jordan.
choices.outcome: Jordan points back to the charter.
choices.why: You have the charter; use it first.

debrief.concept: Late changes cost the most; the charter is your anchor.
debrief.independent: Thank them, reference the agreed scope, and offer an in-scope option now plus a path for later.
debrief.escalateWhen: Escalate if the faculty member insists and the change threatens launch.
debrief.sop: PM SOP: Change of Scope; Drafting a Charter
